lesson.title: The Sharp Bend: Corner Points
lesson.summary: A corner point is a place where a function is continuous but its left-hand and right-hand derivatives exist as different finite numbers, so the graph bends sharply instead of turning smoothly.
lesson.body:
Among the ways a function can fail to be differentiable, the corner point is the most visually intuitive. It occurs at a point a where f is continuous, and where both one-sided derivatives f'_-(a) and f'_+(a) exist as finite real numbers, but those two numbers are not equal. Because both slopes are finite, the graph does not shoot off vertically on either side. Instead, the curve approaches a with one well-defined slope and leaves with a different well-defined slope, and the mismatch between the two produces a visible kink, the way a bent piece of wire has a definite angle rather than a smooth curve at the bend.

This is different from a discontinuity, where the graph is torn apart, and it is different from a cusp or vertical tangent, where at least one side has an infinite slope. A corner is, in a sense, the mildest kind of non-differentiable point: the function is well-behaved and continuous, and each side individually has a completely ordinary tangent line, but the two tangent lines are different lines meeting at an angle rather than merging into one.

Take h(x) = x^2 for x less than or equal to 0, and h(x) = x for x greater than 0. Continuity at x = 0 holds because the left piece gives 0^2 = 0 and the right piece approaches 0 as well, matching h(0) = 0. Now compute the one-sided derivatives. The left piece has derivative 2x, so h'_-(0) = 2(0) = 0, meaning the curve arrives at the origin perfectly flat from the left. The right piece has derivative 1 everywhere, so h'_+(0) = 1, meaning the curve departs from the origin along a line of slope 1. Since 0 does not equal 1, x = 0 is a corner point of h. Unlike the symmetric V-shape of |x|, this corner is lopsided: one side is flat and the other side climbs at a 45 degree angle, but it is a corner all the same because two distinct finite slopes meet there.

Corner points show up constantly outside of textbooks. A car's speed-versus-time graph has a corner wherever the driver switches abruptly from accelerating to braking. A cost function built by taping together two different pricing formulas, such as a flat rate up to some usage level and a different per-unit rate afterward, has a corner at the usage level where the pricing rule switches, unless the two formulas happen to have matching slopes there. In each case, the function is perfectly continuous, meaning there is no jump in value, but the rate of change itself jumps, and that jump in rate is exactly what a corner records.

Recognizing a corner from a formula comes down to the same routine used for any one-sided derivative check: verify continuity first, then differentiate each piece separately and evaluate the one-sided limits at the boundary point. If both limits are finite numbers and they disagree, the graph has a corner at that point, and no single tangent line, and therefore no derivative, can be assigned there.
